China property flow-on effects?
Are you able to elaborate on the Oxford Economics note on the struggling Chinese housing market. Will this have any impact on Australia?- CanVas
Are you able to elaborate on the Oxford Economics note on the struggling Chinese housing market. Will this have any impact on Australia?
Unfortunately Oxford Economics didn't draw any links to Australia.
Very broadly, a meaningful decline in China's property market has implications for the Chinese economy.
Any hit to the Chinese economy has flow-on effects for Australian export demand.
Not sure we can quantify anything on that front at this stage now though.

Oil price up over 2%
The oil price is climbing higher in Asia trade.
Brent crude is up 2.1% to $102.33 at 2:40pm AEDT.
Price pressure is rebuilding due to persistent worries about Middle East supply amid an increase in attacks on shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.
Attacks on tankers sailing through the Strait of Hormuz hit their highest last week of any week since the Iran war began.
The increase in attacks is occurring as more crude is flowing out of the Gulf but at higher costs and risk to cargoes and crew.
Final clearance rate published
Five weeks into the spring season, property data firm Cotality reports that the combined capital clearance rate, at 45.4%, is at its lowest level since July.
Cotality data showed that across the combined capital cities, the 1,212 auctions held last week were 38.1% lower than at the same time last year when 1,958 auctions were held.
Melbourne and Sydney together held 710 fewer auctions than a year ago, accounting for most of the combined capital decline of 746.
Canberra, Perth and Brisbane also held fewer auctions, while Adelaide and Tasmania were the only capitals to hold more.
Melbourne and Sydney both had higher clearance rates than the week before.
Melbourne's clearance rate improved 2.5 percentage points, from 47.9% to 50.4%.
The city held 666 auctions last week, 134.5% more than the 284 held over the Grand Final weekend.
In Sydney, the clearance rate rose 0.9 percentage points to 49.3%, from 48.4%.
Over the long weekend, the number of auctions in Sydney fell 61.4%, from 774 to 299.
Cries for regional full-service bank branches

The Regional Banking Investment Alliance (RBIA) is calling on the industry and federal government to act on its proposal for a community service obligation that it says would "share the cost of keeping regional branches open".

It's survey, just released, shows what it says is "overwhelming support for face-to-face regional banking services, with 95 per cent of respondents rating local bank branches as essential or important to their community".

The survey of 1,555 regional Australians conducted in September and October 2026 found that only 39% of respondents had used Bank@Post and 80% of those did not consider it a sufficient alternative for their banking needs.
Regional Australia Bank chief executive officer David Heine said the results sent a clear message.
“People want a local branch with trained staff they can trust and who know them," he said."They need help with scams, access to cash and somewhere to discuss their finances privately."

Key Event
'[China] housing won't find a floor this decade': Oxford Economics
Oxford Economics has penned a note on the struggling Chinese housing market.
Here are the key takeaways.
• We’re more pessimistic than the consensus about when a floor will form.

• Housing inventories are near record highs, developer financing has been squeezed further, and the exposure of banks to more insidious forms of real estate lending has risen markedly. We expect housing to subtract ~1.6ppt to GDP growth this year and ~1.1ppt next year.

• Against that, the authorities continue to offer incremental demand-side housing support. With recent price recoveries in tier-1 cities proving limited, we also see growing evidence that the property market’s problems are feeding into weaker economic activity – and the reverse is becoming more evident, too, creating an ugly feedback loop.

• But there’ll be no single trough, as resale transactions should recover before prices, and construction will likely bottom out before the housing stock has fully repriced. Less a conventional property cycle and more a structural repair of various balance sheets, the housing adjustment is increasingly likely to take the form of repeated temporary stabilisations rather than a clean cyclical turn.

• Recent mortgage subsidies are too narrowly targeted, and, by our calculations, cheaper financing still can't fully offset expected capital losses. Some frontloaded buying may materialise given the one-year subsidy application window, but more debt isn’t likely given consumers’ currently low appetite for risk.
• Nor can China simply build through the downturn. We estimate total structural demand for housing will be roughly half 2019’s levels by 2035 and fall by another 50% by 2060.

BCCC working to help banks stop making the lives of grieving families harder
So, I've discussed some of the shortcomings of the Banking Code Compliance Committee (BCCC) in an earlier post.
Here's some of the positive elements coming out of its annual report.
"Strengthening management" of deceased estates

Ever since the "I Fee Dead People" scandals uncovered in the Hayne royal commission, banks have tried to stop charging customers that it knows are dead fees for services that can only be accessed by the living.
A further issue has been the at-times diabolical treatment of the relatives of people who have died.
This is not ancient history:
• Between 1 July 2019 to 30 September 2023, ANZ charged fees and interest to deceased estate accounts in error.
• To remediate, ANZ paid approximately $3,253,646 to 18,852 impacted estates.
• In February 2022, ANZ identified a backlog of 7,329 delayed cases of deceased estates.
• ANZ sent approximately 10,604 apology letters to representatives of the estates affected by potential delays. (Some got a small amount of compensation
The bank received the harshest punishment available to the BCCC: it published the name ANZ alongside a report about the wrong-doing. In other cases, it doesn't name the institution.
"We decided to apply a sanction to name ANZ and publish details of its non-compliance on our website and in our Annual Report."
In this year's annual report, the BCCC talks about what it has achieved across the sector, regarding this problem.
"Our report of July 2026, 'Managing deceased estates – a follow-up review', showed that most banks reported changes to their systems, processes, staff training and monitoring arrangements.
"These changes point to more structured and accountable practices, including better identification of relevant products, stronger staff capability and closer oversight.

"Improvements should support more timely processing, reduce the risk of inappropriate fees and other errors, and provide representatives of deceased customers with clearer and more consistent service at a difficult time.
"We found that progress remains uneven, though.
"Some banks still rely on manual processes and have fragmented accountability, while gaps in training and monitoring may limit the impact of the improvements they have made.
"We will continue to monitor the progress of this issue, with a focus on banks that reported changes still under development or not yet fully embedded"

Bendigo Bank says RBA's next move is to pause

Following the Reserve Bank's decision this month to lift the cash rate to 4.6 per cent — its highest level since 2011 and fourth rate rise in eight months -Bendigo Bank says the central bank will now pause.

"Recent economic indicators have highlighted a growing strain on family budgets across Australia, with household spending remaining flat, the ending of the temporary fuel excise relief in August driving transport costs higher and softening residential property prices," Bendigo Bank chief economist David Robertson said.
"These factors have all contributed to a decline in consumer sentiment."

"Unless upcoming employment or inflation data deliver major surprises, we anticipate the cash rate will remain on hold at 4.6 per cent through November and December as we see more signs that demand in the economy is moderating, however there will need to be a lot more progress with inflation before rates can be lowered."
Key Event
Will the government meet its building 1.2m new homes target?

The Urban Development Institute of Australia (UDIA), a lobby group representing Australia's property development industry, says new numbers show the government is off track in meeting it target of building 1.2 million new homes by mid 2029.

It says the latest Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) data shows 47,170 homes were completed nationally in the June Quarter 2026, bringing the total number of homes delivered over the first two years of the National Housing Accord to 355,820.
To remain on track to meet the Accord's 1.2 million national target, Australia needed to have delivered 480,000 homes, leaving it around 124,000 behind after two years.
"While the increase in completions in the latest quarter is encouraging, Australia will need to sustain this momentum to close the gap," said UDIA National President Oscar Stanley.
"On the current trajectory, the shortfall is projected to grow to around 310,000 homes by the end of the Accord."
He said this comes as evidence across the housing industry shows significant numbers of projects in the development pipeline are being shelved or deferred.

"Industry estimates indicate financing capacity for new projects and the spending power of prospective buyers have both been eroded by approximately 10 per cent, while uncertainty around housing values is making it harder for developers, financiers and buyers to commit to new projects," he said.

19,551 breaches, $47 million in financial impact: regulator of banking's code tallies industry problems
The annual report of the Banking Code Compliance Committee (BCCC) has been released.
It notes 19,551 breaches of the Code and $47 million in financial impact on customers.
Breaches of the Code must be reported when they affect more than 20 customers or result in more than $20,000 in financial impact
I've written previously about the BCCC, a well-meaning body that does good work but has few powers and rarely uses them.

The committee was set up in the wake of epic failures with the industry exposed at the Hayne royal commission. It holds members to standards set out in a Banking Code of Practice, a set of guidelines that has no weight in law but is written into the contracts when you buy a product from a bank.
I hope you're sitting down: it's most substantial power is to publish the name of the organisation that it has found in breach of the Code.
And it doesn't even do it that often.

It is funded entirely by the banking industry's key lobby group, the Australian Banking Association, and a few years ago asked for the ability to routinely name banks in breach of the rules, and to force them to publicise it (such as a note on the bank's website).
The ABA said... no thanks.
So it's a body that does solid behind the scenes work but is in no way a watchdog.
Here's what the BCCC's report says about the model of self-regulation that it operates under:
"The Code is a fundamental element of successful self-regulation.
"Self-regulation involves the industry setting its own standards of conduct and enforcing these standards through breach identification, reporting, and remediation.
"This model allows the industry to demonstrate a commitment to ethical and responsible behaviour, helping to build trust with customers.
"It also reduces the need for costly and time-consuming regulatory intervention.
"Our work monitoring the Code is crucial to the success of the self-regulation model working to its full potential."
So either a win for the reduction of red tape, a safeguard for customers, a weak system that shows the strength of the banking lobby in avoiding regulation or a little of all three.
Key Event
HIA attacks ATO proposed ban on tax debts being paid by credit card

The residential construction industry is the latest to attack the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) over an announcement that it will withdraw individuals and businesses being able to pay tax debts by credit card from December 1.
The agency convened a meeting with business groups this week to discuss the changes in the wake of widespread backlash from business groups.

The Housing Industry Association (HIA) says while the ATO's decision does not change the amount of tax owed, it removes one of the tools some businesses use to manage the timing of payments and maintain cash flow.

"HIA is calling on the ATO and the federal government to reverse the decision before it takes effect on 30 November and retain access to credit card payments for taxation liabilities," HIA's chief executive industry and policy Simon Croft said.

"Removing payment flexibility does not reduce a business's tax obligations. It simply makes managing cash flow more difficult at a time when many builders are already facing significant cost pressures."

He said given small and medium-sized builders construct the majority of Australia's new homes, "at a time when governments are looking to increase housing supply, every effort should be made to support the businesses responsible for delivering those homes, not impose further costs and complexities on their business".
Key Event
ASIC issues stop orders following surveillance of private credit market
The corporate watchdog has put stop orders on three private credit funds over concerns that retail investors may have been misled by some of the information on offer.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) has placed interim stop orders that prohibit Australian Secure Capital Fund from offering, issuing, selling or transferring interests in three managed investment schemes — the ASCF Premium Capital Fund, ASCF Select Income Fund and the ASCF High Yield Fund.

ASIC says it made the interim order to protect retail investors from acquiring products under a Product Disclosure Statement (PDS) that "may be defective and not worded and presented in a clear, concise, and effective manner".
The interim stop order arose from ASIC's surveillance of private credit funds.
ASIC said as of June 30, the three funds had $251.8 million in assets under management. Each invest in short-term mortgages secured over Australian property.

"Firms must ensure their disclosures to investors are transparent and support informed decision making, including to help investors understand the strategies and risks of their products," ASIC Commissioner Simone Constant said."We will act swiftly to protect investors from potential harm and promote higher standards across the sector."
